title: Patterns and drivers of understory structure inside and outside of forest reserves in Central Europe
content:
Abstract
Protecting forests is a key conservation strategy, aiming to allow the development of structurally complex forests that provide habitat for diverse species. In fragmented landscapes, small reserves are often easier to establish than large ones, but much of their area lies near the reserve boundary, rendering effects of administrative boundaries on forest structure important. We examined understory structure, a key component of forest structural complexity, along boundary-centered transects in 44 Central European forest reserves using terrestrial lidar, contrasting conditions inside vs. outside protected areas for recently designated reserves and reserves established 45 years ago. Specifically, we (i) described forest understory structure across different forest types (i.e. riparian, upland, and mountain forests), and (ii) examined how protection status, time since designation, proximity to reserve boundary, and landscape features influence understory structure. We mapped forest structure across 236 transects (40.8 km total length; 80.4 ha of area), quantifying indicators of vegetation height, density, connectivity, and vertical diversity within the first 10 m above ground. Understory characteristics inside reserves did not differ from adjacent managed forests in most cases. Understory structure in reserves designated >45 years ago was not clearly different from that in recently established reserves. Near the reserve boundary, understory structure was moderately more complex than 100 m inside or outside protected areas, likely reflecting boundary placement along features such as streams or roads. Even after decades of protection, the understory structure of forest reserves did not differ strongly from their managed surroundings, highlighting the long lead times of conservation measures in forests. Our findings suggest that management around reserves follows a “close-to-nature” approach mimicking natural processes. For selecting potential future reserves, the development stage at the time of protection, as well as the boundary location, should be considered explicitly to ensure desired conservation outcomes.
